posts.title: "No FX fee" is one of the most useful lines on a crypto card page, and one of the easiest to misread.
posts.author: TxSpend
posts.snippet:
"No FX fee" is one of the most useful lines on a crypto card page, and one of the easiest to misread.

Of the 49 crypto cards TxSpend tracks, 17 publish a flat 0% foreign exchange fee. The other 32 either charge one or do not state a flat 0% rate.

Three things worth checking before you rely on that label:

- Billing currency. Check which currency the card bills in. If you pay in a different currency, a conversion still happens, and its cost can sit in the exchange rate rather than in a fee line.
- Conversion from crypto. Moving stablecoins or other tokens into the card balance can carry its own spread or fee, separate from the FX fee.
- Tiers and regions. Some issuers set different fees by region or card tier, so the headline rate may not be the one that applies to you.

At TxSpend, a card is labelled "no FX fee" only when the issuer's own page publishes a flat 0% rate. Conditional or partial waivers do not count.

posts.title: Zoom, the BBC, HSBC, IKEA and GitLab didn't get hacked on Monday.
posts.author: Ojas Vyas
posts.snippet:
Zoom, the BBC, HSBC, IKEA and GitLab didn't get hacked on Monday.
Their visitors did.

On 16 November, an attacker got write access to the custom JavaScript inside Optimizely Web projects. For about 16 hours, Optimizely's own CDN served that code to visitors of 178 organizations.

It swapped crypto wallet addresses on copy, skimmed card numbers from payment forms, lifted cookies, and tried to push exploit kits to older iPhones.
Nobody's perimeter was touched. The script came from a domain every one of these companies had deliberately allowlisted.

The number that stuck with me: Scott Helme's team at Report URI checked the affected sites' Content Security Policies. Roughly 15% had one strict enough to stop this. 68 had none at all.

Three things I'd check this week on any site running third-party tags:
1. Where can a script on your checkout page send data? Everyone tunes script-src. connect-src is what stops the exfiltration. And nonce + strict-dynamic would not have saved you here: it trusts whatever a trusted script loads.
2. Is card entry inside a cross-origin hosted iframe? This skimmer couldn't read those.
3. Who can edit your experimentation or tag manager project, and would anyone notice a change? These tools ship production code with no code review.

If you run Optimizely Web: review the Project JavaScript field in every project and audit your users and API tokens.

Your A/B testing tool has the same access to your checkout page as your own developers. Most companies have never threat-modelled it.

If you want a second pair of eyes on what your third-party scripts can do, my DMs are open.

posts.title: El cliente que te dice “eres caro” no está comparando precios. Está comparando riesgos.
posts.author: Piedad Calderón
posts.snippet:
El cliente que te dice “eres caro” no está comparando precios. Está comparando riesgos.

Cuando un cliente potencial te dice “es que la competencia me cobra la mitad” o “se me sale de presupuesto”, la reacción instintiva de muchos profesionales es defender la tarifa, hacer un descuento o justificar cada partida de la propuesta.

Si entras a discutir el precio, estás aceptando su premisa: que tu servicio y el de la competencia son commodities intercambiables.

La realidad es que el precio casi nunca es la causa principal del rechazo. Es el síntoma de una falta de percepción de valor y de un riesgo no gestionado.

Cuando tu propuesta parece "cara", suele ocurrir por una de estas 3 razones:

No ha medido el coste de NO resolver el problema: El cliente ve lo que le cuesta contratarte, pero no ha calculado cuánto le cuesta seguir como está durante los próximos 6 meses.
Está comparando peras con manzanas: No entiende la diferencia entre un servicio transaccional (más barato) y una solución estratégica.
Busca una excusa diplomática: Para no admitir que no confía del todo en el resultado o en su propia capacidad para implementarlo.

¿Cómo responder sin bajar tus tarifas?

Desplaza el foco del coste de la solución al coste del problema: “Entiendo que el presupuesto es clave. Pero antes de hablar del coste del proyecto, déjame preguntarte: ¿cuánto le está costando a la empresa mantener esta ineficiencia cada mes?”

Haz evidente la brecha de riesgo: “Puedes encontrar opciones más económicas en el mercado. La diferencia es que nuestra propuesta incluye [garantía/acompañamiento/metodología] para asegurar que el proyecto no se quede a medias.
¿Es la inversión inicial tu única duda o hay algún resultado específico que quieras asegurar?”

No compitas por ser la opción más barata. Compite por ser la opción que transmite más certeza y menor riesgo.

Quien compra por precio, se va por precio. Quien compra por certeza, se queda por valor.

¿Cómo la objeción del precio cuando aparece?

posts.title: Ayer se cumplió un año de uno de los días más especiales y gratificantes de mi trayectoria académica y profesional: la defensa de mi tesis doctoral.
posts.author: Mercedes Fernández Ríos
posts.snippet:
Ayer se cumplió un año de uno de los días más especiales y gratificantes de mi trayectoria académica y profesional: la defensa de mi tesis doctoral.
Ese 17 de noviembre de 2025 fue un día que significó mucho más que la culminación de una etapa académica. Fue un día en el que me sentí profundamente acompañada, arropada y querida por todas las personas que, de una manera u otra, formaron parte de ese camino.
Emprendí este recorrido desde el amor y la pasión por mi profesión, guiada por unos valores que mis padres me inculcaron: el trabajo, la constancia, la perseverancia y el servicio a los demás. No fue un camino exento de dificultades, hubo momentos de incertidumbre, momentos en los que caí, pero siempre tuve muy presente la capacidad de trabajo y sacrificio de mis padres, por ellos, tuve la fuerza de levantarme, seguir adelante, continuar caminando y afrontar las dificultades que encontré durante el camino. también hubo siempre una razón 
En este recorrido tuve la enorme fortuna de contar con el apoyo incondicional, la orientación y el acompañamiento de mis directoras de tesis, Rosa Redolat  y Emilia Serra a quienes quiero dar el mayor de los agradecimientos. Su confianza, cercanía y generosidad fueron fundamentales durante todo el proceso.
Ayer, al recordar aquel día, comprendí una vez más el verdadero significado de esta palabra: recordar, volver a pasar por el corazón. Y, al hacerlo, volví a sentir la emoción, la felicidad y la satisfacción de aquel momento, pero, sobre todo, volví a conectar con aquello que da sentido a mi trayectoria: la pasión por mi trabajo.
Una pasión que va mucho más allá del conocimiento científico o de los logros académicos; que se construye cada día en el encuentro con las personas, en el acompañamiento, en la escucha y en el compromiso con quienes conviven con algún tipo de demencia. Porque es precisamente en ese contacto humano donde la ciencia encuentra su razón de ser y donde la vocación profesional adquiere su significado más profundo.
La investigación, el conocimiento y su divulgación cobran verdadero sentido cuando conseguimos acercarlos a la realidad de las personas y contribuir, desde nuestra profesión, a mejorar su calidad de vida y la de quienes las acompañan.
Hoy quiero celebrar no solo un logro académico, sino también los valores que lo hicieron posible: el esfuerzo, la perseverancia, la gratitud, la vocación y el servicio a los demás.
Gracias a todas las personas que formasteis parte de aquel día y de este camino.

posts.title: Anthropic sale a bolsa esta semana. ¿Está cara a 1,4 billones de dólares? 🧵
posts.author: Guillermo Abellán Berenguer
posts.snippet:
Anthropic sale a bolsa esta semana. ¿Está cara a 1,4 billones de dólares? 🧵
 
Hoy Anthropic, la creadora de Claude, fija el precio de su OPV (rango de 70–78 $) y mañana empieza a cotizar en Nasdaq con el ticker ANT. He analizado su folleto de salida (el S-1) y hemos proyectado ("con la ayuda de Claude y Gemini ) su valoración a 10 años. 

Estas son las conclusiones 👇
 
1️⃣ Las pérdidas “astronómicas” son sobre todo contables

Perdió 80.700 M$ en el primer semestre, pero 72.400 M$ son un ajuste contable de sus bonos convertibles, que suben de valor cuando sube la valoración de la empresa. No es dinero que haya salido de caja. De hecho, en el tercer trimestre generó 6.600 M$ de caja operativa.
 
2️⃣ Dos negocios en uno
 
Servir los modelos (la inferencia) deja un margen bruto cercano al 85%.

Entrenar el siguiente modelo es inevitable: el 80% de los ingresos viene de modelos con menos de 6 meses.

Contando todo el cómputo, el margen real baja a alrededor del 42%.
 
3️⃣ El crecimiento es histórico, pero se está frenando.

 17.000 M$ de ingresos en el tercer trimestre (+1.127% interanual). Pero el crecimiento trimestral bajó del 144% al 47%, y el trimestre volvió a tener pérdida operativa (−567 M$).
 
4️⃣ El riesgo real: unos 895.000 M$ en compromisos de cómputo

 Son contratos con Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Broadcom y SpaceX, entre otros. Si la demanda se frena, esas facturas siguen llegando.
 
5️⃣ Qué espera el mercado

El libro de órdenes está unas 6–7 veces sobresuscrito. En Hyperliquid, el contrato perpetuo de ANT cotiza en torno a 98 $, un +25% sobre el máximo del rango.
 
6️⃣ Proyección a 10 años (vídeo)

 A 78 $, Anthropic cotiza a unas 21 veces sus ventas, casi como Nvidia (22x), pero sin sus márgenes. En el escenario base, sus ventas se multiplican por 8 hasta 2036 y su precio/ventas cae de 20,7x a 6,9x, hasta un nivel similar al de Meta hoy. Eso equivale a una rentabilidad de alrededor del 10,7% anual comprando a 78 $.
 
📌 Conclusión

 A 78 $, Anthropic no es cara si cumple el plan, pero sí lo es si no lo cumple. Su precio ya descuenta un crecimiento que ninguna empresa de su tamaño ha conseguido nunca. Comprar a unos 98 $ el primer día deja todavía menos margen de error.
 
Las dos cifras que hay que vigilar cada trimestre:
 → ¿Se estabiliza el crecimiento de las ventas?
 → ¿Mejora el margen después de pagar el cómputo?
 
Si las dos van bien, la valoración se justifica. Si fallan, el ajuste lo hará el precio.
 
¿Vais a entrar en la OPV o esperaréis a ver los primeros trimestres? 👇

posts.title: Day 7/20 — A security token is a security first. A token second.
posts.author: Maarten Van Doorslaer
posts.snippet:
Day 7/20 — A security token is a security first. A token second.

One of the biggest misconceptions I still encounter in tokenisation is that tokenised securities are somehow a new category of crypto assets. They're not.

A regulated security token is, first and foremost, a security.
Not a utility token. Not a stablecoin. Not an NFT.

And that distinction has enormous consequences for how you structure an investment product. At Rubey, we experienced this firsthand. When we structured our first tokenised investment product in 2020, we chose Luxembourg.

At the time, Luxembourg offered a legal framework that allowed us to use blockchain-based securities registers. We structured the investment as a debt instrument. A few years later, following developments in Belgian company law, we were able to establish a different structure in Belgium. This time, we opted for an equity-based model using a Belgian maatschap (partnership).

Two different jurisdictions. Two different financial instruments. Two different legal structures. Both had advantages. Both had disadvantages.

And that brings me to one of the most important lessons I've learned:
There is no perfect legal structure for a tokenised investment. There are only trade-offs.

One of the first things you need to consider is taxation. Not just at the level of the investment vehicle, but also at the level of the individual investor. A structure that works well for one investor profile may be considerably less attractive for another.

And your target audience matters. Are you targeting private investors through a private placement? A broader retail audience through a public offering? Or a combination of both? Those choices influence the legal, regulatory and tax considerations from the very beginning.

But there's another dimension that is still too often overlooked. What happens when investors want to sell their tokens before the underlying asset is sold?

Structuring the primary issuance is one challenge. Structuring the investment so that secondary transfers are legally straightforward and tax-efficient is another. A structure that works perfectly well when investors subscribe may become significantly less attractive when those same investors start trading their interests.

And even after you've invested considerable time and money in getting everything right, tax legislation can change. A structure that was carefully optimised at launch may require reconsideration just a few years later. That's the reality of regulated tokenisation.

The blockchain may be immutable. The legal and tax environment certainly isn't.

Which is why I believe legal and tax structuring should never be treated as an administrative exercise to complete before issuing tokens. It is a fundamental part of the investment proposition. And it needs to account for the entire investment lifecycle.

¿Cómo transforma el voluntariado los programas de las administraciones públicas? 🤝🏛️

Un estudio publicado en la revista Administrative Sciences por investigadores de la Universidad de Sevilla (Fran Santolaya Soriano, Mateus Uchôa e Isidro Maya-Jariego) analiza cómo la acción voluntaria mejora el ajuste comunitario y la eficacia de las políticas públicas en Andalucía.

La investigación evidencia que no existe un modelo único de gestión, sino que las estrategias deben adaptarse al rol del voluntariado. Identifica tres modalidades principales en la administración pública:

1️⃣ Agentes en educación de iguales (Efecto multiplicador). Programas como Forma Joven o Corresponsales Juveniles muestran que formar a jóvenes con habilidades comunicativas permite difundir mensajes preventivos y de salud de forma natural, multiplicando su alcance entre pares. 
2️⃣ Campos de voluntariado y emplazamientos internacionales (Desarrollo de competencias). Iniciativas como los Campos de Voluntariado, el Cuerpo Europeo de Solidaridad o Erasmus+ priorizan el aprendizaje intercultural, la convivencia, la autonomía y el desarrollo de competencias cívicas y profesionales. 
3️⃣ Eventos deportivos y apoyo social comunitario (Aumento de la capacidad operativa). Programas como Liga LED, Mentor10 o la red Contigo aportan apoyo logístico, mentoría y acompañamiento emocional, haciendo viables grandes eventos o intervenciones contra la soledad no deseada.

💡 ¿Qué aporta realmente el voluntariado a los programas públicos? Más allá del apoyo puntual, la integración estratégica del voluntariado permite a las administraciones dos grandes logros:

Movilización de recursos comunitarios. Desarrolla los principios de participación y complementariedad, mejorando la cobertura, la sostenibilidad y la adecuación cultural de los servicios a la realidad local.

Ampliación de la capacidad operativa. Incrementa la capacidad logística en el desarrollo de actividades y promueve el aprendizaje y las competencias de participación ciudadana.

📌 Esta investigación se enmarca en el seguimiento y evaluación del I Plan Integral de Voluntariado y Participación Ciudadana de Andalucía (Horizonte 2026), financiado por la Secretaría General de Familias, Igualdad, Violencia de Género y Diversidad de la Junta de Andalucía a través de la Fundación de Investigación de la Universidad de Sevilla (FIUS). El trabajo ha sido posible gracias a la colaboración de personas voluntarias, entidades coordinadoras y personal técnico de la administración autonómica, con el apoyo clave de Inmaculada de la Rosa en la monitorización de las políticas públicas de voluntariado en Andalucía.

🏗️⚖️ Mantenimiento e inspecciones obligatorias: Lo que toda comunidad debe saber para evitar sanciones.

La seguridad de un edificio no es opcional, y la responsabilidad de su mantenimiento recae directamente sobre la Comunidad de Propietarios. Desde el @Colegio Profesional de Administradores de Fincas de Madrid (CAFMadrid), recordamos la importancia crítica de las inspecciones periódicas a través de Organismos de Control Autorizado (OCA).

¿Por qué es vital estar al día?

Industria no avisa. Es deber de la comunidad solicitar las inspecciones de instalaciones eléctricas (REBT) y de protección contra incendios (RIPCI) en los plazos legales. Ignorar estos plazos puede derivar en sanciones que superan los 8.000 €.

Puntos clave a vigilar:

⚡ Instalaciones Eléctricas: Cada 10 años en edificios de viviendas con potencia >100 kW (o más de 16 suministros en la Comunidad de Madrid).
🔥 Protección contra Incendios: Cada 10 años en garajes, trasteros o locales comerciales de más de 500 m².

El consejo del experto: No basta con reparar los defectos tras una inspección "condicionada". Es obligatorio comunicar la subsanación a la OCA para obtener el certificado favorable. No hacerlo a tiempo es el motivo más común de multas elevadas, incluso si la obra se hizo.

La gestión profesional del Administrador de Fincas es la mejor garantía para la seguridad de los vecinos y la salud económica de la comunidad.

posts.title: Kandidaten skal kunne forklare hullet i sit CV, men Ingen forklarer hullet i vurderingen.
posts.author: Sofie Jagert
posts.snippet:
Kandidaten skal kunne forklare hullet i sit CV, men Ingen forklarer hullet i vurderingen.

Local Law 144 fra New York burde være pensum for alle, der arbejder med rekruttering. Loven har været håndhævet siden 2023, men jeg mener at den fortjener langt større opmærksomhed, særligt nu, hvor AI får stadig større indflydelse på, hvordan vi vurderer mennesker. I New York City skal virksomheder informere kandidater på forhånd, når de anvender automatiserede værktøjer såsom AI i rekrutteringen. De skal blandt andet oplyse, hvilke kvalifikationer og egenskaber værktøjerne vurderer, og sikre, at de er undersøgt for mulig diskriminerende skævhed.

Når vi rekrutterer, beder vi mennesker om at fortælle os, hvem de er. Vi forventer ærlighed, selvindsigt og evnen til at forklare de valg, der har formet deres arbejdsliv. Den åbenhed fortjener at blive gengældt.

Enhver vurdering er samtidig præget af vores egne forestillinger om dygtighed. Af de spørgsmål, vi stiller, de erfaringer, vi tillægger værdi, og de muligheder, vi forestiller os, at et menneske rummer. Vi kan kende et menneskes arbejdshistorik til mindste detalje og stadig have forstået forbløffende lidt af dets potentiale.

Efter mange år med udvikling af HR-tech kender jeg dets muligheder. Jeg ved også, hvor let vores antagelser kan få karakter af sandheder, når de omsættes til kriterier, data og systematiske vurderinger. Ensartethed er værdifuld, men ingen garanti for retfærdighed.

Jeg mener, at vi skal stille lige så store krav til vores egen dømmekraft som til den teknologi, vi tager i brug. Kandidater bør kende grundlaget for deres vurdering, have mulighed for at tilføre deres erfaringer den nødvendige sammenhæng og vide, at nogen kan forklare og stå på mål for beslutningen.

Local Law 144 er værd at kende, fordi den minder os om, at retten til at vurdere andre mennesker også indebærer et ansvar for at gøre det med omtanke, åbenhed og respekt.

posts.title: Last week I ran a workshop in Paris for boutique law firm leaders.
posts.author: Chris Dias
posts.snippet:
Last week I ran a workshop in Paris for boutique law firm leaders.

Adviserly invited me to host the Legal Tech & AI Circle session at Boutique Pioneers 2026, "Taking responsibility for AI: supervision and best practice". Boutique law firm leaders came from the UK, Europe, Turkey, the US and India: founders who put their own names above the door, joined by the tax, compliance and legal content specialists they work alongside. Every one of them answers personally for the work that leaves their firm.

That is what makes AI such a hard question for them. The agenda is being set by tech companies and Big Law. Meanwhile the courts in England and Wales have already referred lawyers to their regulators over AI-generated citations that did not exist, and the pattern emerging is that the supervising solicitor is also held to account, not just the person who drafted the work. A boutique firm cannot afford to get this wrong, and it cannot afford to sit it out.

So we spent the session deciding. There were five topics every firm is now deciding on, whether it means to or not: supervision, client disclosure, pricing, use cases and investment. Each had five cards, from the sceptic to the early adopter. Teams chose, the room debated, one final card for each topic. Every card had to pass one test: could a boutique firm adopt this within the first six months of using AI? I was given forty minutes. It ran for almost an hour (sorry!)

I designed the workshop to test whether other boutique firms shared my concern about where to draw the line for AI in law, given how highly regulated and specialised our work is. It was that concern that led me to author the professed.ai manifesto and to publicly declare Lawyery as an AI-Hybrid firm.

What came out of the workshop is the Adviserly AI Adoption Policy: five guidelines written by the people who will have to live with them. The code is advisory only, and by its nature it is a compromise reached by the room. But it is valuable data on how boutique firms are navigating these potentially treacherous waters, and if you are a lawyer in a boutique firm, it is worth knowing.

Starting tomorrow I will post one topic a day, covering the card the room chose, the cards it turned down, and why it matters. Supervision first. The full policy will then be published on the Adviserly and professed.ai websites.

Lawyery are proud members of Adviserly. My session was one part of a carefully curated programme at Boutique Pioneers 2026, designed to inform, engage and make a real difference to the firms taking part, and everyone left Paris with fresh energy and the confidence that the boutique way is the future of law. My thanks to Robert Flint, Kellie Simpson and the Adviserly team, and to everyone in the room.  

I am excited to share the results on Linkedin first before official publication.  See you tomorrow!

It was a privilege to attend the PPM Tech Law Seminar. The speakers were exceptionally well prepared, and the discussions were insightful and thought-provoking, particularly around AI, technology, and the evolving legal landscape.
  
What stood out for me, beyond the excellent presentations, was seeing how PPM Attorneys is investing in the next generation of legal professionals.
  
I had the opportunity to engage with several law students from various universities, including UNISA, and those conversations left a lasting impression on me.
  
It was sad to hear about the challenges these young people face trying to enter the job market. They have invested years in their education, yet many struggle to gain practical experience or simply get their foot in the door.
  
What saddened me, however, also inspired me. Despite these challenges, their determination, resilience, and willingness to put themselves out there were remarkable. They are actively seeking knowledge, building networks, and doing everything they can to create opportunities for themselves.
  
This is where PPM Attorneys deserves special recognition. By making events like this freely accessible to students, they are doing more than sharing industry knowledge. They are creating a steppingstone, giving young people access to professionals, meaningful conversations, and networking opportunities that could shape their careers.
  
It also made me reflect on my own journey.
  
Most of us were once in their shoes. We didn't always have the experience, connections, or opportunities. Somewhere along the way, someone believed in us, offered guidance, made an introduction, or simply gave us a chance.
  
Someone opened a door for us. The question is, whose door are we opening today?
  
Sometimes, one conversation or introduction can change the direction of a young person's career. We may not all be in a position to offer employment, but we can certainly offer encouragement, mentorship, and access to our networks.
  
Well, done to the entire PPM team for an excellent seminar and, more importantly, for creating opportunities for our future professionals.
  
Our young people are not short of ambition or potential. They simply need more people willing to give them a chance.

posts.title: Nigeria is bringing stablecoins into the regulatory framework. But not everyone will be able to enter the market.
posts.author: Victor Yaromin
posts.snippet:
Nigeria is bringing stablecoins into the regulatory framework. But not everyone will be able to enter the market.

On 5 November, the Central Bank of Nigeria introduced new rules for stablecoins and other non-security virtual assets, creating a much clearer framework for businesses operating in the country.

I went through a new legal guide from Kiet Business Attorneys, and a few things stand out. 

Official Link: https://lnkd.in/emeehfaS

The entry barrier is high.
Stablecoin issuers will need ₦10 billion in capital for naira-backed coins and ₦15 billion for foreign-currency stablecoins. Exchanges, wallets and other service providers face a ₦1 billion minimum.

Stablecoins will have to meet strict reserve requirements.
Issuers must maintain full backing plus an additional 2% buffer, provide redemption at par, and undergo regular reserve attestations. Yield on stablecoin holdings is prohibited.

P2P trading isn't disappearing, but it is changing.
Platforms facilitating P2P transactions will need appropriate licences and specific CBN approval. Naira-to-stablecoin conversions will also face tighter controls and authorised channels.

Existing operators have a transition period, with registration required by 5 December 2026 and full licence applications due by 4 May 2027.

Nigeria is making a clear choice. It wants stablecoins to remain part of its financial ecosystem, but under a framework that prioritises capital, compliance, consumer protection and control. This could make the market more trustworthy. At the same time, the requirements may push smaller players out and make partnerships with licensed institutions increasingly important.

The interesting question now is how much of Nigeria's existing stablecoin activity will move into the regulated market, and how much will adapt to these new rules.

Thank you Emmanuel Eyo and Abdul-Malik Yerima

posts.title: How to Choose the Right AI Tool for Your Business
posts.author: Carmen Jara Wittich
posts.snippet:
How to Choose the Right AI Tool for Your Business

The AI market is growing rapidly. New tools, platforms and solutions appear almost every day.

But choosing the right AI tool is not about following trends or buying the most advanced technology.

It is about finding the solution that creates real business value.

Before investing in an AI tool, I would evaluate seven key dimensions:

1. Business Needs & Objectives
What problem are we trying to solve? Which processes could benefit from AI? Define the business requirements before exploring tools.

2. Business Value & ROI
Will the solution reduce costs, improve productivity, support better decisions or enhance customer experience? Define measurable outcomes.

3. Functionality & Use Cases
Does the tool actually meet your requirements? Avoid paying for features your organization will never use.

4. Integration & Scalability
Can it integrate with existing systems and workflows? Will it support future business needs without creating unnecessary complexity?

5. Security, Data Protection & Compliance
Where is company data processed and stored? How is sensitive information protected? Consider access controls, data privacy, regulatory requirements and AI governance.

6. Total Cost of Ownership
Look beyond subscription fees. Include implementation, integration, training, maintenance, support and ongoing usage costs.

7. Vendor Strategy & Exit Options
Evaluate the provider's financial stability, support, roadmap, contractual flexibility and potential vendor lock-in.

One important consideration:

The best AI tool is not necessarily the most powerful, the most popular or the cheapest.

A sophisticated platform can create little value if employees don't adopt it, processes aren't ready or the business case is unclear.

This is where IT, Procurement, Finance, Legal, Security and business stakeholders need to work together.

Procurement can play a strategic role by challenging requirements, comparing providers, evaluating commercial models and ensuring sustainable vendor relationships.

My key takeaway:

Don't start with: "Which AI tool should we buy?"

Start with: "What business problem do we want to solve and is AI the right solution?"

Technology should follow business needs, not the other way around.

How does your organization evaluate AI tools: based on functionality, cost, security or measurable business value?

posts.title: You're doing this wrong if you think copyright protects your idea. 🤯 This is one of the most common and potentially costly misconceptions we encounter, especially among brilliant i
posts.author: Trilect Associates
posts.snippet:
You're doing this wrong if you think copyright protects your idea. 🤯 This is one of the most common and potentially costly misconceptions we encounter, especially among brilliant innovators and ambitious startups ready to disrupt the market.

Many believe that simply having their groundbreaking idea documented – whether in a pitch deck, a concept note, or a detailed blueprint – automatically grants them legal protection against others using that core concept. The truth is, copyright law has a very specific job: it protects the *expression* of an idea, not the idea itself.

Think about it this way: Copyright shields your original book manuscript, the unique lines of code in your software, or the distinctive design of your product's user interface. It doesn't, however, prevent someone from taking the *underlying principle* or *core concept* of your idea and expressing it in their own unique way. That's a significant vulnerability for any creator or business relying solely on copyright for their main innovation.

So, how do you truly safeguard that ingenious concept, that revolutionary business model, or that breakthrough technology? This is where other critical Intellectual Property avenues like patents, trade secrets, and strategic confidentiality agreements become your most powerful allies. Ignoring these means leaving your most valuable asset exposed and risking your competitive edge.

Don't let a misunderstanding about copyright leave your innovation vulnerable. Understanding the right IP strategy for your specific idea is absolutely crucial for long-term success and sustainable growth. Let's ensure your groundbreaking ideas are protected, not just expressed.

posts.title: Everyone is predicting the death of offshore exchanges this week. I don't think that's what's happening.
posts.author: Zoe Y.
posts.snippet:
Everyone is predicting the death of offshore exchanges this week. I don't think that's what's happening.

What's happening is slower. Crypto is changing what it rewards.

For most of this industry's life, regulation was treated as a tax on speed. The venues that won were the ones that listed first, asked the fewest questions and sat furthest from any regulator.

That made sense when the risk people feared most was missing the next 100x.

It makes less sense after you've lived through an exchange collapse and a withdrawal freeze with nobody to call.

Licensed exchanges in the US have existed the whole time. Webot for one, holds MSB licenses across 48 states. Nobody wrote threads about it. Compliance is boring until the week it isn't.

The tradeoff is real. Licensed venues list fewer tokens, and they move slower. Plenty of projects still run on legal opinions they haven't touched since mainnet.

That used to look like a weakness. I'm no longer sure it was. It may just have been a cost the market wasn't ready to price.

So here's what I keep thinking about: if the next cycle rewards trust over speed, how many of today's project were only ever built for speed?

posts.title: 🛂 5 questions every bank asks a crypto company
posts.author: Roman Okonenko
posts.snippet:
🛂 5 questions every bank asks a crypto company

1. "What exactly does your business do?"
Prepare a one-page description and a simple flow of funds diagram. The bank should see where the money comes in, where it goes and who handles it.

2. "Do you need a licence?"
Show the licence and its scope. If you don't need one, the best answer is a letter from the regulator confirming it. A legal opinion also helps, but banks trust the regulator more.

3. "Who owns the company, and where does the money come from?"
An ownership chart down to the beneficial owners, plus source of funds and source of wealth. If the money comes from crypto, add wallet history and exchange statements.

4. "Who are your clients?"
Client types, countries, restricted jurisdictions, expected volumes and average transaction size. The more specific, the better.

5. "How do you manage AML risk?"
AML policy, a named compliance officer, KYC process, sanctions screening, blockchain analytics and transaction monitoring.

Banks don't expect a crypto company to be risk-free. They expect it to know its risks and explain them clearly.

One more tip: make sure your answers match your website. Banks check. 🗂️
posts.reason: Practical guidance on banking requirements for crypto companies invites discussion and directly reaches founders and compliance leads dealing with CASP and regulatory questions.

comments.text: Worth adding a sixth, because it's the one that trips up applicants most: under MiCAR, a bank or payment provider will also ask whether you're relying on a white paper notification or an actual CASP authorisation - the first is a filing, the second is a supervisory approval, and conflating the two in your pitch to a bank reads as a red flag, not reassurance.

Controls and South Korea AI Exam Cheating Scandal

1. The Case
On 15 Nov 2026, Han Won-seok, No.1 scorer in Korea's Certified Tax Accountant exam, confessed he photographed questions with a micro-camera in glasses, sent them to Generative AI, and read answers on a smartphone. He got 159/160 in Round 1. Two proctors and HRD Korea review caught nothing.

This happened 4 days before CSAT / Suneung, the national university exam for 551,864 students on 19 Nov 2026. In Korea, Suneung decides university and career. Trust collapsed.

2. Control Framework

A. Preventive - Stop it before
Old: Phone ban, 2 proctors per room. Failed because smart glasses were only banned in July 2026 and no search was done.
New for Suneung: Total ban on phones, smart glasses, watches, rings, earphones. Bags in corridor. Stickers on clothing buttons. Sleeves rolled up. Glasses inspected on desk. Wi-Fi blocked inside and near schools.

B. Detective - Catch it during
Old: Human proctors cannot see a 2mm camera. No RF detectors.
New: 8,400 extra staff + 75,000 proctors at 1,312 sites. 1,800 smart-device specialists. Hotline from centre to Ministry for instant decisions. Metal detectors. Future: 7,200 RF detectors, 6.57bn won budget. But offline on-device AI emits no signal, so RF alone will fail.

C. Corrective - Punish after
Old: Score cancelled + 1-year ban. Too weak.
New: Score cancelled + 10-year ban. Criminal complaint for obstruction, up to 5 years prison. University admission cancelled even after admission. Investigation of device sellers and AI app logs.

3. Why Controls Failed
1. Control lag: Tech moved faster than law.
2. Over-reliance on humans.
3. Single control = single failure.
4. No anomaly detection: 159/160 was not flagged.
5. Weak deterrence.

4. Ideal Model
Multilayered defence, as proposed by Prof. Choi: Combine Physical + Optical + RF + Behavioural + Oral verification. No single control works.

Sudarshan Aithal v. Bank of India & Ors.
**NCLAT, Principal Bench, New Delhi
 Brief Facts
The appeal challenged the NCLT order dated 14.05.26 admitting the Sec 7 IBC application against Distribution Logistics Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. The Corporate Debtor defaulted on its loan and was declared NPA. Despite settlement proposals, the upfront amount was not deposited. The debt was subsequently assigned to JM Financial ARC.
2. Grounds of Appeal
- The lenders had entertained and accepted the OTS proposal of ₹590 crore.
- Higher settlement offers of ₹625 crore and ₹631 crore were made but rejected.
- Rejection of settlement proposals and assignment of debt were alleged to be unfair.
- CIRP would adversely affect the Corporate Debtor and its employees.
- An opportunity to settle the debt ought to have been granted.
3. Defence
- Financial debt and default were admitted.
- The OTS was conditional upon deposit of ₹59 crore upfront, which was not paid.
- Repeated settlement commitments were not honoured.
- Acceptance or rejection of OTS was within the commercial wisdom of lenders.
- Admission under Section 7 was justified upon establishment of debt and default.
4. Analysis by the Tribunal
The Tribunal held that debt and default were undisputed and the scope of Section 7 was limited to examining the existence of default. The Appellant failed to deposit ₹59 crore under the OTS and also failed to honour subsequent offers, including the direction to deposit ₹631 crore in two instalments. 
Settlement proposals did not extinguish the default, and the lenders could not be compelled to accept the OTS. 
Withdrawal of CIRP was also subject to amended Section 12A.
5. Final Order
The appeal was dismissed. The NCLT was held to have correctly admitted the Section 7 application. No order as to costs.
 Analysis
The decision reiterates that admission under Section 7 principally depends upon financial debt and default. Unfulfilled OTS proposals do not defeat CIRP, particularly where the Corporate Debtor repeatedly fails to honour settlement commitments.
Ratio:
Once debt and default are established, failure to honour conditional settlement proposals does not constitute a ground to set aside admission of CIRP.

A radar that emits nothing cannot be found by the thing it is looking for.

BAE Systems has built one, and it listens to your television signal to work.

Compare the Cloud follows defence and infrastructure technology where it touches the wider tech market, and this is a clear example of reusing signals that already exist.

Engineers at BAE Systems have developed a passive radar that detects and tracks airborne threats without revealing its own position. The company says it is up to ten times cheaper than many current passive radar systems.

A conventional radar transmits, and that emission can give away its location. This one transmits nothing. It picks up existing digital TV, radio and mobile network signals and uses them to find and follow objects, so it stays invisible in the radio frequency domain.

It is small enough to deploy from an SUV, tracks targets from small drones to larger aircraft, and builds a 3D air picture with speed, heading, range and altitude. BAE sees uses for police, the protection of critical national infrastructure and the military.

There is a civilian angle too. At airports and infrastructure sites, active radar is often restricted because of its emissions, and a passive system can run without disturbing existing electromagnetic activity.

Live trials with law enforcement, defence and critical infrastructure partners run throughout 2027.

posts.author: Linh Phùng

From Magic Crossbow to AI Chips: The Honey-Trap Problem

Jensen Huang is not alone in facing security scrutiny over personal relationships. He resigned as Nvidia CEO on 12 November 2026 amid reports of affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected by US intelligence of Chinese links. Crucially, espionage has NOT been established.

Vietnam has a 2,000-year-old cautionary tale: Princess My Chau and Trong Thuy.

1. ACCESS: After failing to defeat Au Lac's powerful crossbows (Au Lac is a former name of Vietnam), Zhao Tuo proposed peace and marriage between his son, Trong Thuy (Vietnamese name of Zhao Tuo's prince), and Vietnamese King - An Duong Vuong’s daughter.
2. TRUST: The couple grew close. The king welcomed Trong Thuy as his son-in-law and gave him access to the royal household.
3. DISCLOSURE: During private conversations, Trong Thuy asked why Au Lac was militarily unbeatable. My Chau showed him the sacred crossbow and its trigger mechanism.
4. THEFT: In one telling, he arranged a replica trigger, swapped it during a family gathering and carried the secret back to his father.
5. TRACKING: Before leaving, he asked how to find her if war broke out. She promised to scatter goose feathers along her route.
6. COLLAPSE: The crossbow failed in battle; the feathers exposed the royal escape route. The king killed his daughter; Trong Thuy later died by suicide.

This is LEGEND, not a proven espionage case. But archaeology at Co Loa has uncovered bronze crossbow triggers, tens of thousands of three-edged bronze arrowheads, casting remains and extensive spiral fortifications. The military technology was real; the plot remains legend.

Nor is relationship-based espionage uniquely Chinese. Shi Pei Pu and French diplomat Bernard Boursicot were convicted of espionage in 1986. Soviet intelligence exploited US Marine Clayton Lonetree’s relationship. East Germany’s Stasi deployed “Romeo spies” against officials and secretaries with access to sensitive information.

A 2018 article by Major General Duong Duc Thien in Vietnam’s National Defence Review recommends security training, vetting sensitive roles, managing exposure risks, protecting documents and systems, and regular checks for vulnerabilities.

For SME tech founders, translate that into:

- Least-privilege access to source code, models and customer data.
- Protected API keys, admin accounts and audit logs.
- Partner due diligence and confidential reporting channels.
- Evidence-based security checks, never profiling by nationality or private relationships.

Read the 2018 research before your startup scales. Better to learn from Co Loa than discover your own “magic crossbow” has been copied.

In defence of media copyright
By Rod Sims*
The media’s role is fundamental to our society and our democracy. It is more important than ever at this time of social media effectively encouraging polarisation and resentment.

This is why I am worried about the Government seemingly wanting to remove the benefits of copyright from media content.
Let’s look at what we know.

Brent Hecht, Microsoft’s director of applied science, in an internal email, has described AI scraping and training practices in relation to media articles as “the largest theft of labour in human history”. He is correct! 

Yet the major tech firms argue that Australia’s copyright laws create a hostile environment for technology growth. Jason Kwon, from OpenAI, has warned that copyright issues will determine whether AI companies invest billions in Australia or not. That is, legalise the theft or we will not invest in Australia.
The AI companies make two arguments.

First, it is said that Australia’s copyright laws are out of line with international norms. Yes, in some minor ways but in these circumstances irrelevant. When it comes to AI taking media work the impact of copyright law appears to be the same in Australia and the US and overseas generally. 

This is why in the US there are over 150 court cases where AI companies are being sued by rights holders for breach of copyright. 

AI companies are seeking to weaken or remove copyright protection in Australia in ways they cannot achieve in the USA or elsewhere. 

Second, it is said that it’s too hard for AI companies to do deals with every rights holder. But there are a finite number of large media companies and collective deals can then be done with smaller players. 

As an obvious example, Country Press Australia represents 107 different publishers and 237 member newspapers.

AI companies seem unwilling to engage with far fewer suppliers than supermarkets Coles or Woolworths do on a regular basis.

Currently, the AI companies can either do voluntary commercial deals – bilateral and collective – to gain access to content, or rights holders can take court action when their content is taken without consent.

There are over 200 announcements of licensing deals covering over 8000 media companies around the world. So voluntary commercial deals are happening overseas.

It appears that the Government is aiming to remove copyright protection by the following steps.

Most patent portfolios are designed for yesterday's company.
  
When a company first starts building a patent portfolio, the priorities are often clear. Protect the core technology. Secure the breakthrough. Demonstrate that there is something valuable to invest in. And at that stage, that often makes perfect sense.
  
But companies evolve. The challenges facing a business raising its first investment round are rarely the same as those facing the same business a few years later. New products emerge. Manufacturing becomes more important. New markets are explored. Competitors become easier to identify, partnerships are formed, and freedom-to-operate considerations become more significant.
  
Yet it's surprisingly common for a patent portfolio to remain heavily focused on the company's original priorities. The result can be a disconnect between the technology that was important when the business started and the technology that is driving value today.
  
Some of the most interesting intellectual property discussions I've had aren't actually about a new invention. They're conversations with companies that have grown significantly since filing their first patent application and are starting to think differently about what really creates competitive advantage. Where is the business heading? What capabilities now create competitive advantage? What would a competitor most want to copy? The answers are often very different from those that would have been given a few years earlier.
  
The strongest patent portfolios aren't static. They evolve alongside the business, the technology and the competitive landscape.
  
A portfolio that was right for yesterday's company isn't necessarily right for today's.

The challenge is not a lack of AI opportunities. It is turning AI potential into measurable business value.
Looking at manufacturing, transportation, and oil and gas, I see enormous potential for AI, particularly in knowledge management, advanced analytics, engineering simulation, and decision support.
Yet, as Gartner's research highlights, the strength of AI adoption and use cases varies significantly across industries.
In my view, five challenges need greater attention:
🔹 Unclear ROI: We need better ways to measure value beyond productivity gains, including operational efficiency, risk reduction, asset reliability, and engineering performance.
🔹 Domain-specific AI: Generic AI alone is unlikely to address the complexity of industrial environments. AI must understand engineering principles, operational processes, and industry-specific requirements.
🔹 Confidence and trust: Industrial adoption depends on accuracy, explainability, reliability, and confidence in AI-generated outcomes.
🔹 Security and assurance: Data protection, intellectual property, safety, and governance are fundamental requirements, not afterthoughts.
🔹 Combining AI skills with domain expertise: Perhaps the most important challenge. AI expertise without deep industry knowledge will struggle to deliver meaningful industrial transformation.

My view: The next breakthrough in industrial AI will not come from more powerful models alone, but from combining domain knowledge, trusted AI, and measurable business outcomes.

The opportunity is enormous. The question is whether we are building the right capabilities to unlock it.

posts.title: The minimum legal stack every founder should have in place before chasing the next round of anything.
posts.author: Hauwa Umar
posts.snippet:
The minimum legal stack every founder should have in place before chasing the next round of anything.

I once came across something that made me rethink how many founders approach building a business.

A founder can spend months perfecting a product, building a team, attracting customers and preparing for investment.

But ask where the company’s original intellectual property is assigned, or whether the founders have a written agreement about ownership, and suddenly, the answers become less certain.

Not because the business isn’t doing well.

But because some important conversations were postponed while everyone was busy building.

And that’s where problems begin.

Before chasing the next investor, signing a major partnership or expanding the team, there are a few legal foundations worth getting right.

For starters:

1. Incorporation documents: Make sure your company’s share structure, ownership records and statutory documents are accurate and accessible.
2. A founders’ agreement: If you’re building with someone else, don’t rely entirely on friendship and verbal understanding. Agree on responsibilities, equity, decision-making and what happens if someone wants out.
3. Intellectual property assignments: Ensure the business actually owns the work created for it, including code, designs, content and other intellectual property.
4. Employment and contractor agreements: Put expectations, confidentiality, ownership of work, termination and other important terms in writing.
5. Privacy policy and terms of service: Your documents should reflect how your product actually operates and how you collect, use and protect customer information.
6. A contract register: Keep track of the agreements you’ve signed, your obligations, renewal dates and important deadlines.
7. An organised document repository: Know where your corporate records, contracts, licences and compliance documents are stored.

Here’s what I think founders sometimes underestimate:

Legal documentation isn’t just something you prepare when an investor requests it.

It’s part of building a business that can withstand growth.

You don’t want your first serious conversation about ownership, intellectual property or contractual obligations to happen when a potential investor is already examining your business.

Get the foundations right while things are still manageable.

Founders, save this and audit yourself against it this week.

#StartupLegal #Founders #LegalOperations #DueDiligence #Compliance #StartupAdvice

posts.title: Crypto and VAT: HMRC's new guidance in plain English
posts.author: Swabi
posts.snippet:
Crypto and VAT: HMRC's new guidance in plain English

In October, HMRC published new guidance (GfC21) on VAT and cryptoassets. The headline: there are no special VAT rules for crypto. What matters is what you're actually selling.

If you take crypto as payment
VAT works the same as if you were paid in pounds. You charge VAT on your goods or services as normal, based on their sterling value at the time of sale.

If you sell NFTs
VAT follows whatever the NFT represents. A digital artwork NFT is usually treated as a digital service, so VAT depends on where your customer is based.

The blockchain won't tell you what you need
A wallet address doesn't show where a buyer lives or whether they're a business. HMRC expects you to collect that information yourself. For sales to consumers in other countries, you need two pieces of evidence of where they live.

Selling through a platform?
If the platform sets the terms, collects customer details and takes payment, it's usually responsible for the VAT. If buyers pay you directly, the VAT is your responsibility.

Keep records
Record the sterling value of every sale and who you sold to. Getting it wrong can lead to backdated VAT, interest and penalties.

posts.title: 🤔.....Forced administration for unfair practices generally refers to either statutory intervention into an organization due to systemic misconduct or external administration in cor
posts.author: TROY.L. PARRISH
posts.snippet:
🤔.....Forced administration for unfair practices generally refers to either statutory intervention into an organization due to systemic misconduct or external administration in corporate insolvency intersecting with regulatory breaches. Because the exact mechanism depends on the entity involved, Australian law addresses this across three primary contexts.
1. Statutory Administration of Unions or Associations
Under Australian industrial law, governments or courts can place a registered organization (such as a union) into external administration if it engages in systemic unlawful or unfair conduct.

Legislative Intervention. Parliament can pass targeted legislation or apply to the Federal Court to appoint an independent administrator to take control of an organization's management, finances, and operations.

Cooperation Mandates. Officers, employees, and advisers are legally compelled to hand over records and cooperate with the administrator. Refusing to comply or obstructing the process carries severe financial penalties.

Governance Reset. The administrator has the power to remove officials, restructure internal rules, and investigate misconduct to restore lawful governance.

2. Corporate Insolvency and Regulatory Breaches
For private companies, "forced administration" usually means court-ordered liquidation, receivership, or ASIC intervention rather than voluntary administration, which is initiated by the company's own directors.
Regulatory Enforcement. Regulators like the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) and the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) can pursue heavy civil penalties against companies engaging in unfair trading practices, misleading conduct, or unconscionable behavior.

Insolvency Triggers. If court-ordered fines or consumer compensation orders render a company unable to pay its debts, creditors or regulators can apply to the court to wind up the company and appoint a liquidator.
Ongoing Legal Claims. Entering external administration does not automatically shield a business from accountability for unfair workplace practices. The Fair Work Commission has established that an administration stay does not automatically block employees from pursuing unfair dismissal or general protections claims.
3. Local Government and Public Bodies
In the public sector, state governments have statutory powers to suspend elected councillors or board members and appoint an official administrator.
Triggering Conduct. This typically occurs following an independent inquiry that uncovers systemic governance failures, financial mismanagement, or unfair administrative practices.
Interim Control. The appointed administrator assumes all decision-making powers of the council or board until new elections can be held or governance standards are met.

We see export control questions land on legal desks only after a shipment has already stalled at customs — building that classification discipline into procurement and sales from the start, as this role seems structured to do, is the right sequencing.
